tip: 'Precisar' needs 'de' before its object: 'precisariam de quantas cadeiras', how many chairs you would need.
'Torcer' literally means to wring, but 'torcer para' is the verb for rooting for a team: 'torço para que o Brasil ganhe'.
'Confiar' pairs with 'em', and 'em' plus 'ele' contracts to 'nele': 'confio nele' means I trust him.
'Embora' means although and always takes the subjunctive: 'embora ela seja jovem', not 'é jovem'.
'Valer a pena' means to be worth the trouble: 'valha a pena reclamar' means worth complaining.
In Portuguese you have haste ('ter pressa') rather than being in a hurry, so 'não precisa ter pressa' means no need to rush.
'Prestar atenção' (pay attention) takes 'em': in 'presta atenção no que', 'no' is the contraction of 'em' plus 'o'.
'Lembrar' (to remember) normally takes 'se' and 'de', with 'de' plus 'o' contracting to 'do': 'ele se lembre do meu aniversário'.
'Experimentar' usually means to try or taste, not to experiment: 'experimenta esse bolo' means try this cake.
'Respire fundo' means take a deep breath: the adjective 'fundo' (deep) does the adverb job here, no '-mente' ending needed.
When the person might not exist, the verb after 'que' goes subjunctive: 'ninguém que fale', not 'fala'.
'Mesmo que' means even if and takes the subjunctive: 'mesmo que você tente', not 'tenta'.
'Antes que' means before and triggers the subjunctive: 'antes que eu esqueça', not 'esqueço'.
English can leave the preposition at the end ("friends I went out with"); Portuguese puts it up front: 'com quem saí'.
The ending '-inho' shrinks and softens a word: 'minutinho' is a little minute, meaning just a quick moment.
A positive command to a friend is 'toca', but negating it flips to the subjunctive: 'não toque'.
'Largar de' plus a verb is a casual way to say stop doing something: 'larga de ser teimoso'.
'Deveria' (should) is the conditional of 'dever' – softer than 'deve'.
As the object of a preposition, use 'mim', not 'eu': 'pra mim' means for me.
Spoken Brazilian Portuguese normally puts the object pronoun before the verb, even at the start: 'me conta'.
'Fazer as pazes' is a set phrase meaning to make up or make peace: 'faz as pazes com ela'.
'Precisar' takes 'de' before what you need: 'precisar de passaporte'.
The conditional ending '-ria' turns a question into a polite offer: 'aceitaria um café'.
'Antes de' is followed by the plain infinitive, not a conjugated verb: 'antes de começar'.
With body parts Portuguese normally uses the article, not a possessive: 'os dentes' here means your teeth.
'A gente' means we but takes a singular verb: 'a gente está'.
'Vamos' plus an infinitive says what we are going to do: 'vamos conversar' = we'll talk. It also works as a suggestion: 'Vamos comer?'
The verb 'pôr' is irregular; its command form is 'põe': 'põe a roupa'.
'Levar' means to take away from the speaker; 'trazer' means to bring toward the speaker: 'leva o cachorro'.
'Guardar' usually means to put away or store, not to guard: 'guarda a louça'.
